title: Nataraja explained
hook: under the planted foot lies a small figure on his belly, and the dancer never finishes him off

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the elephant hand pointed to the lifted foot, and left the walking to you. Where did you point instead of push? Today, the other foot, and who's under it. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.
screen: `IT POINTS, AND LEAVES THE WALKING TO YOU.` · `TODAY: UNDER THE FOOT.`

segments.voice: He's the easiest part of the image to miss. Look down past the swinging arms and the flying hair to Nataraja's right foot, the planted one. Under it, flat on his belly, lies a small, round-limbed figure, often holding a snake, pinned to the ground. He isn't the hero of anything. He's closer to the name that was right there a second ago, or the reason you walked into this room, gone. Small, daily, and back again no matter how many times you shoo it out. His name is Apasmara.
screen: `EASY TO MISS.` → `UNDER THE PLANTED FOOT.` → `HIS NAME: APASMARA.`

segments.voice: In the usual reading, Apasmara is ignorance, the forgetfulness that hides what's true, the mind losing hold of itself. There's a story behind him, told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram and retold by the art historian Ananda Coomaraswamy. Out in a forest lived a community of sages, proud of their own rites, who thought they had no need of Shiva. He came among them in disguise, and they were furious. So they used their powers against him. First they sent a tiger. Shiva caught it, peeled off its skin, and wore it around his waist. Then they sent a snake. He hung it around his neck like a garland. Then they sent a dwarf, a malicious little creature. Shiva put his foot on its back, and began to dance. And the sages, watching, gave up their pride. Now here's the detail worth carrying home. Shiva never kills Apasmara. He doesn't kick him off the stage, or crush him. He just keeps him under the foot, and keeps dancing. Some readers say that's honest about forgetting. It doesn't go away for good, not in this life. It has to be kept down, gently, again and again. Some go further and say if forgetfulness were destroyed outright, nobody would have to make the effort of remembering, and the effort is part of the path. Either way, the dancer isn't anxious about it. The calm face we started with sits right above the foot that holds forgetting down. Remembering isn't a victory you win once. It's a dance step you keep taking.
screen: `APASMARA: FORGETTING, IGNORANCE.` · `TIGER, SNAKE, DWARF FROM THE SAGES.` · `HE IS HELD DOWN, NEVER KILLED.` · `THE EFFORT IS PART OF THE PATH.` · then, large: `REMEMBERING IS A STEP YOU KEEP TAKING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the planted foot. Sit with both feet flat on the floor, and let the breath slow. Feel the right foot's weight, the heel, the ball, the toes. Let your attention rest there. Sooner or later it will wander off into a plan or a memory. That's Apasmara, and it's fine. When you notice, press the right foot gently into the floor, the way the dancer's foot holds the small figure down, not hard, just enough to feel it. Then let the attention settle back into the foot. Each press is a step in the dance. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, every time you come back. The bell holds the time.
Nataraja explained. Today, Apasmara under the planted foot: forgetting, held down and never killed, so that remembering stays a step the dancer keeps taking.

Your line: Nataraja explained. Today, pick one thing you keep forgetting, and put a small reminder where you'll see it. Then don't be hard on yourself when you forget anyway. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: In Nataraja images the right foot rests on Apasmara, a small figure read as ignorance or forgetfulness; the story of the forest sages, the tiger, the snake and the dwarf is told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram.

fork.setup: you're the dancer. the sages have sent a malicious dwarf against you, and now he's under your foot. what do you do?
options: crush him once and for all.
keep him under your foot and dance.
fork.reveal: Shiva keeps Apasmara pinned and dances. some readers say forgetting can't be finished off once; it has to be held down again and again.

original.note: Sanskrit: Apasmara, the figure under Nataraja's foot, read as forgetfulness and ignorance.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shiva is stepping on an enemy.
what it means: forgetfulness, held down and never killed, so remembering stays a step you keep taking.
what a scholar hears: the Tamil tradition calls the figure Muyalakan, and Coomaraswamy reads him as ignorance, held down by the dance.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
the year just walked and kept

sources.ref: Nataraja images: Apasmara under the right foot (iconography described)
The forest sages, the tiger, the snake and the dwarf (Chidambaram temple tradition)
sources.work: Ananda K. Coomaraswamy, The Dance of Shiva (1918) (paraphrased)

notes: The forest-sages story (often the Daruka or Taruka forest; tiger, snake, dwarf) follows Coomaraswamy's retelling in 'The Dance of Shiva', which cites the Koyil Puranam. Some tellings add a deer, fire or other attacks; kept to three. Confirm.

Apasmara 'linked with forgetting': the Sanskrit lexicon gives forgetfulness, loss of memory and epilepsy for apasmara. Confirm wording. Tamil name given as Muyalakan (also Muyalaka); confirm spelling.
'Often holding a snake' describes many bronzes; confirm.
The two readings of why Apasmara isn't killed are framed as 'some readers'; they are popular interpretations, not from a cited text.
